rows.mainText: Home / Digital legacy resources Set up provider arrangements alongside your map Apple Legacy Contact and Google Inactive Account Manager have different triggers and limits. Record your arrangements without copying access or recovery secrets into your map. Written by Rillora · Updated 18 October 2026 On this page Each provider controls its own process Apple: a designated contact for certain account data Google: choices triggered by account inactivity Record what you arranged and where to check it Keep the two sets of choices aligned Each provider controls its own process A map helps someone find an account and understand your wishes. A provider's settings determine what its own service may do. Setting up one does not configure the other. Check the official instructions for your account and region, and review the arrangement when the provider, your contact or your circumstances change. Apple: a designated contact for certain account data Apple's Legacy Contact can request certain account data after the account holder's death. The request requires the access key and the documentation Apple specifies for the country or region. This does not include iCloud Keychain passwords, passkeys or payment information. Follow Apple's instructions for handling the access key; record a location or next step in your map instead of copying the key into it. Google: choices triggered by account inactivity Google's Inactive Account Manager can notify chosen people or share selected data after a configured period of inactivity. The account holder chooses the recipients and data. Inactivity is a different trigger from a documented death. Review the choices in Google itself; recording a wish in Rillora does not turn that Google setting on or change it. Record what you arranged and where to check it A useful record names the provider, notes that an arrangement exists and explains where its instructions are kept. Add when you last checked it and who should be contacted. A fictional entry could say: “Photo account; provider legacy contact configured; instructions kept with the household documents.” Leave the access key, password and recovery codes out. Keep the two sets of choices aligned If you change a designated contact at the provider, review the corresponding person and record in your map. If you revoke a Rillora invitation, that does not remove a designation made directly with Apple or Google. Check both places deliberately. The official links below are the starting point for current availability, instructions and limits. rows.mainText: Home / Digital legacy resources Choose a tool for the job you need it to do Compare a document, a password manager, provider settings and a digital legacy map by the information they hold, who can see it and how you can change or leave the arrangement. Written by Rillora · Updated 18 October 2026 On this page Write down the problem before comparing features A document or spreadsheet can be a starting point A password manager has a different responsibility Provider settings apply to that provider's account A digital legacy map connects matters, wishes and people Check the parts that matter before relying on it Write down the problem before comparing features Do you need a list of important matters, a protected place for sign-in secrets, a provider-specific arrangement, or a way to show different people different records? These are separate jobs. A product that solves one may still need to work alongside the others. Judge it by a real example from your situation rather than the longest feature list. A document or spreadsheet can be a starting point A simple document can record provider names, locations and wishes. Its sharing and revision controls depend on where you keep it. Before using it, decide how the intended person will find the current version and which copies may continue to exist. Do not turn that convenient list into a collection of complete credentials. A password manager has a different responsibility A password manager is designed around sign-in secrets. Recovery and emergency-access options vary by product, so read the provider's current documentation. A list of logins may still leave questions about which document matters, what you would prefer someone to do, or where an original record is held. Provider settings apply to that provider's account An account provider may offer its own designated-contact or inactivity settings. Those settings do not organize all your other accounts, paper documents and devices. Keep a record of the arrangement, then use the provider's own process for changing it or making a request. A digital legacy map connects matters, wishes and people Rillora organizes important matters and location hints and lets you choose the records and details shared with a recipient. It is intended as a map, not a password vault. Consider this approach when the main problem is helping the right people understand where to start while keeping unrelated matters private. Check the parts that matter before relying on it Try a harmless example. Check the recipient's view, whether they can use the web, how to revoke access and what happens to existing copies. Read the storage and recovery explanation, export options, current price and cancellation terms. An information-sharing feature should not be presented as legal authority, guaranteed account access or an automatic transfer of ownership. Write the provider or institution and a useful location hint. A file location or a masked identifier can be enough; avoid putting full credentials into the record. Separate your wishes from permission Describe what you would like someone to do and where they should look for the appropriate process. Knowing that an account exists, having permission to act, accessing the account and transferring ownership are separate steps. Your map does not replace a will, provider requirements or legal advice for your circumstances. Choose the person and the information Decide who needs to see each matter and how much detail helps them. Check their view before sharing. Someone who only needs to know that a document exists does not necessarily need its contents or the details of your other matters. Review the map after an account, document location or relationship changes. A missed sign-in is not evidence of death and should not release information automatically. Example: an insurance document A fictional record could say: “Home insurance; policy document in the household files; ask the insurer about the appropriate claim process.” Share that record with the person who needs it. This points them towards the next step without promising that they can access or claim the policy. rows.mainText: Home / Digital legacy resources Share a useful starting point, with a clear boundary Choose who needs each digital matter, share only the relevant information, check the recipient's view and understand what revoking access can and cannot do. Written by Rillora · Updated 18 October 2026 On this page Agree on what the person is there to help with Choose the matter and the level of detail Example: one household document, not the whole map Check the view and use the intended person's own account Revisit access when the purpose or relationship changes Agree on what the person is there to help with One person may need to find household documents; another may understand a particular online service. Begin with that purpose rather than giving everyone the same collection of records. Ask whether the person is willing to help and explain that receiving information does not automatically give them legal authority or permission to use your accounts. Choose the matter and the level of detail Review each selected matter before sharing it. A name may be enough to explain that something exists; a location hint or recorded wish may be needed for the next step. Unrelated matters should stay outside the recipient's view. Do not add passwords or recovery secrets to make an invitation feel more complete. Example: one household document, not the whole map Suppose you want a family member to know where an insurance document is kept. Share the policy's description, its location and the appropriate contact. They do not need the details of an unrelated device, subscription or financial account. The useful test is whether this one record tells them where to start without exposing the rest of your affairs. Check the view and use the intended person's own account In Rillora, choose the matters and details for a recipient, then check their view before sending an invitation. They sign in with their own account and accept the invitation. A secure web entry is available, so receiving selected information does not require installing the iOS app. Verify the intended person and destination before sharing a link. Revisit access when the purpose or relationship changes Remove access when it is no longer appropriate, and review the remaining records after a significant change. Revocation stops future access through that sharing relationship; it does not erase a screenshot, download or copy someone already made. Discuss confidentiality before sharing rather than relying on revocation to undo an earlier disclosure. Common questions Does the recipient need to install an app? No. Rillora provides a web entry for the recipient to sign in and accept the invitation using their own account. Will revoking access remove an earlier download? No. It stops future access through the relationship. Information already copied or downloaded remains outside that control. rows.mainText: Home / Digital legacy resources What is a digital legacy? Your digital legacy includes the accounts, files, devices and digital affairs someone may need to understand after your death. A useful plan explains where to start. Written by Rillora · Updated 18 October 2026 On this page Start with the things someone would need to find Include locations and wishes, not just accounts Separate finding information from having authority A small example is more useful than an empty master list Prepare now and review when something changes Start with the things someone would need to find Think of the email account connected to household services, family photographs, an important document stored online, or a subscription that keeps renewing. The task is to make these matters understandable to the right person. A list of account names alone rarely explains which information matters or what that person should check next. Include locations and wishes, not just accounts For each matter, record the provider, a safe location hint, your wishes and the person who should know about it. Physical documents and devices can belong in the same map: a paper policy, the location of a laptop, or contact details for someone who holds the originals. Leave passwords, complete recovery codes, private keys and seed phrases out. Separate finding information from having authority Being told where a document is kept does not make someone its owner. Seeing an account name does not authorize a login or transfer. Your trusted contact, a provider's designated contact and a legally authorized representative may have different roles. Record those distinctions so the map directs people to the appropriate provider or professional instead of promising access. A small example is more useful than an empty master list A fictional entry might read: “Family photographs; cloud photo service; ask the provider about the account owner's existing legacy arrangement.” A separate entry could point to a printed insurance policy and the insurer's contact details. These are finding aids, not login credentials or instructions to bypass account controls. Prepare now and review when something changes Start with one matter, check that its location is still accurate, then decide which information another person actually needs. Rillora provides a private map for these records and selected sharing. Long-term absence, loss of contact, incapacity and death should not be treated as the same event; a missed sign-in alone is not proof of death. Common questions Is a digital legacy plan a legal will? A Rillora map organizes information and wishes. It does not itself create a valid will, appoint a legal representative or transfer ownership. Requirements depend on the matter, provider and applicable law. Do I need to share my passwords to start? No. Start with provider names, document locations and appropriate next steps. Keep sign-in and recovery secrets in the systems intended to protect them. rows.mainText: 首页 / 数字遗产整理方法 什么是数字遗产？ 数字遗产包括你身后可能需要由他人了解的账号、文件、设备与数字事务。整理的重点，是让合适的人知道从哪里开始。 Rillora 编写 · 更新于 2026年10月18日 本文内容 先想想，对方需要找到什么 除了账号，也记录位置和意愿 能找到资料，不代表有权操作 先写清一件事，比留下空白总表更有用 现在开始，变化后再复核 先想想，对方需要找到什么 绑定家庭服务的邮箱、存放家人照片的云端相册、保存在网上的重要文件，或持续续费的订阅，都可能需要有人了解。整理这些事务，是为了让合适的人看懂它们。只有一串账号名称，通常还不足以说明哪些资料重要，以及下一步应该核对什么。 除了账号，也记录位置和意愿 每项事务可以记下平台或机构、安全的位置提示、处理意愿，以及应该知情的人。纸质保单、设备存放地点、保管原件的联系人，也可以放进同一份地图。不要写入密码、完整恢复码、私钥或助记词。 能找到资料，不代表有权操作 知道文件放在哪里，不等于拥有这份文件。看到账号名称，也不代表可以登录或转移其中的资产。你信任的人、平台指定的联系人，以及具有合法授权的代表，可能承担不同角色。把这些区别写清楚，让地图引导对方联系相应平台或专业人士，而不是承诺一定能够访问账号。 先写清一件事，比留下空白总表更有用 一条虚构事项可以写成：“家庭照片；云端相册；向平台了解账号持有人已经设置的遗产联系人安排。”另一条事项可以记录纸质保单的位置及保险公司的联系方法。这些是查找线索，不是登录凭据，也不是绕过账号保护的指示。 现在开始，变化后再复核 从一项事务开始，确认资料位置仍然准确，再决定对方需要知道多少。Rillora 用私密事项地图整理这些记录，并按你的选择共享。长期没有使用账号、失去联系、失能和去世是不同情况；一次漏登或长时间未登录，都不能单独作为死亡证明。 常见问题 数字遗产清单就是具有法律效力的遗嘱吗？ Rillora 事项地图用于整理资料和意愿，本身不会建立有效遗嘱、任命法定代表或转移所有权。具体要求取决于相关事务、平台规则及适用法律。 开始整理前，需要先分享密码吗？ 不需要。先记录平台名称、文件位置和适当的下一步。登录与恢复秘密应留在专门保护这些信息的系统中。 继续阅读 一份家人能用得上的数字遗产清单 先看要解决什么，再选择整理工具 了解 Rillora 事项地图 了解共享与安全边界
